claims.text: The baseline alloy is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can be processed using powder-metallurgy routes involving gas-atomized powder, mechanical alloying, and spark plasma sintering.
The proposed equiatomic powder-metallurgy baseline has a single-phase BCC structure.
Composition effects can be studied by systematically increasing Hf while reducing one or more other elements to preserve a total of 100 at.%.
Mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering is suitable for fabricating the proposed non-equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr series.
Limiting oxygen pickup is relevant to controlled powder-metallurgy processing of HfNbTaTiZr.
XRD and SEM can be used to characterize the phases and microstructure of powder-metallurgy HfNbTaTiZr.
TEM, nanoindentation, and tensile or compression tests are established characterization methods for the proposed composition series.
Increasing Hf content modifies the alloy's lattice parameters.
Increasing Hf content increases lattice distortion in HfNbTaTiZr.
Increasing Hf content may increase dislocation density.
Hf has a larger atomic radius than the other relevant constituents and therefore introduces greater lattice strain when its fraction is increased.
Greater lattice distortion enhances solid-solution strengthening.
The increased lattice distortion hinders dislocation motion.
Hindering dislocation motion increases hardness.
Hindering dislocation motion increases yield strength.
Moderately Hf-enriched HfNbTaTiZr will have higher hardness and yield strength than the equiatomic alloy.
Sufficient deviation toward higher Hf content may cause secondary-phase or precipitate formation.
Secondary-phase formation may alter ductility and overall mechanical performance.
The predicted strengthening trend is limited to a single-phase BCC compositional stability region and should be strongest before secondary phases become significant.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as increasing Hf relative to an equiatomic 20 at.% baseline, but the proposed series includes 15 at.% Hf, which is a decrease from that baseline.

The hypothesis and boundary explicitly allow secondary phases after sufficiently large composition changes, whereas the falsification rule treats immediate deleterious secondary-phase formation as falsifying a stronger claim of strengthening 'without adverse effects.' The rule does not distinguish moderate enrichment within the stated boundary from enrichment beyond it.
